extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers working on ensemble casts (novelists, short-story authors, screenwriters)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for creating and shaping ensemble casts: choosing who belongs, how each member is differentiated by role/skill/personality, avoiding stereotypes, and engineering the inter-character conflict and growth that makes an ensemble feel necessary and meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every ensemble member must be meaningful (have a reason to be there)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make every member of the ensemble meaningful: why are they there? What do they do? How are they different from each other and what is each one bringing to the table?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask what skills, baggage, or traits each character contributes. If a character can be removed without changing the story, they are not pulling their weight. Example guidance: identify each member's job in the plot (leader, hacker, etc.) and their personal contribution (emotional glue, chaos-bringer, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Start from story purpose when choosing ensemble members
rubrics_metrics.description: Figure out 'what the story is about' first; once you know the story's central problem, you understand who needs to populate your world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the ensemble decision happens at the start or later in drafting — sometimes you realize mid-draft that a single protagonist can't carry the plot and must add others. Use the story's needs to determine which roles/skills are required (e.g., heists require specific jobs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate plot-role functions from characterization archetypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between the role a character performs in the plot (hitter, hacker, grifter, mastermind) and the characterization archetype/personality they present (the elegant one, the loose cannon, the peacemaker).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't assume a plot role implies a personality; mix and match to avoid predictability (e.g., the elegant grifter, the maternal cold warrior). Considering both axes helps prevent stereotypes and gives texture to the cast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign clear plot-function roles when the plot requires them
rubrics_metrics.description: When the plot demands specific jobs (especially in genre setups like heists), give characters distinct job-related skill sets that accomplish necessary plot tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Leverage-style roles (hitter, hacker, grifter, thief, mastermind) or heist-specific specialists. Ensure each job is plausible and contributes to accomplishing the mission; otherwise consolidate or remove roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate characters by skills, personalities, and the chaos they bring
rubrics_metrics.description: Make characters distinct in terms of skill sets, personalities, and the type/level of chaos or conflict they introduce to the group dynamic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about who brings tension or unpredictability versus who is the stabilizer. Use those differences to generate friction, plot complications, and complementary teamwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stereotypes; interrogate unconscious copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether an archetype is actually a stereotype or an unconscious re-creation of characters you've seen before (e.g., repeating culturally specific tropes like many black superheroes having electrical powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interrogate your motives: 'Am I doing this because I've seen it somewhere before?' If so, find ways to freshen or subvert the expectation. Anti-pattern: recycling favorite characters without change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subvert or combine archetypes to create freshness
rubrics_metrics.description: Take familiar archetypes and alter them or add sub-archetypes (e.g., make a mentor also be dopey comic relief; make a stoic warrior also function as the group's maternal figure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unexpected combinations to surprise readers and deepen characterization — examples include a dopey comic who occasionally drops real wisdom, or a cold warrior who is also the group's caretaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineer ensemble conflict so members must come together
rubrics_metrics.description: Design ensembles so the members have to work at cohesion — they shouldn't start as a unified, harmonious team; their differences should force them to come together through friction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'braided roses' idea: give each character a vital strength (rose) and thorns that irritate others; braid them so the thorns poke each other and produce conflict that drives growth. This conflict should be purposeful and related to story stakes, not gratuitous fighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include emotional/group-dynamic archetypes separate from plot roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the group's emotional or social roles (leader, peacemaker/glue, younger/in-need-of-protection, foil) in addition to their plot functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These roles shape interpersonal dynamics and reader empathy. Example: one character may be the leader in the plot but emotionally insecure, another may be the glue who keeps the team together despite conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not every pair must conflict — use relationships without friction for texture
rubrics_metrics.description: You don't need every character to butt heads with every other character; having stable or allied relationships (sidekicks, inseparable partners) adds texture and contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately create constellations of agreement and disagreement (e.g., Danny Ocean and his sidekick rarely fight) to vary group dynamics and avoid monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure characters are differentiated and not redundant copies
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid creating ensemble members who are essentially the same person; each should bring distinct abilities, viewpoints, or symbolic roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two characters feel interchangeable, recombine, remove, or deepen one to fill a unique niche. Use distinct backstory, archetype, or a sub-archetype to separate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use archetypes to set and manage reader expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that archetypes create expectations in readers; use that to your advantage but manage or subvert those expectations deliberately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you signal a familiar archetype, either fulfill that promise or intentionally subvert it to produce surprise. Be mindful that signaling a stereotype can shortcut characterization but risks predictability or offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider symbolic/representational functions of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand what each character represents in the larger story (or mythic/symbolic terms — orphan, mentor, innocent, trickster), not just what they do practically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mapping characters to larger symbolic roles can clarify theme and emotional resonance (e.g., Kaz as orphan/leader, Wylan as innocent). Use symbolism to deepen stakes and reader investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical exercise: identify and alter archetypes to increase nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework: identify the archetype of each character in your work-in-progress, then change that archetype or give them a sub-archetype to create rounder, unexpected characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an actionable revision technique: pick one character, assign a different archetype or an additional sub-archetype, and see how that change affects interactions and plot. Example: turn the cold, emotionless warrior into the group's maternal figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide ensemble scope and timing intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that the decision to make a story an ensemble can come at different stages (beginning, mid-draft), and that choice affects character introduction and development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you add ensemble members late, ensure their motivations and roles are integrated organically; if planned from the start, use early beats to establish each member's distinctiveness and necessary function.
